**Holding and operative rule:** Congress may punish willful post-enactment failure to pay a legally fixed past-due child-support obligation when the obligor and child reside in different States, because §228 directly protects that cross-border economic payment obligation. The different-state relation is essential to this holding; the Court sustains neither regulation of every family debt nor federal creation or revision of the underlying support duty.

**Authority:** Justice O'Connor's opinion of the Court, Parts I–IV, is joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. This common nine-Justice coalition controls every holding and the affirmance in both prosecutions.

**Controlling explanation:** Section 228(a) requires willful failure to pay a past-due support obligation for a child residing in another State. Section 228(d)(1) requires an amount fixed by a court order or State-law administrative process for support of a child, or a child and custodial parent, unpaid longer than one year or exceeding $5,000. Those thresholds are alternatives; the indictments happen to allege both. Neither the amount nor duration substitutes for the interstate relation.

The object regulated is the required cross-border payment itself. Different residence does constitutional work because the existing obligation calls for satisfaction between the obligor and children in another State. That is a legal characterization of the charged class, not a finding of actual transfer. A completed payment need not precede an offense addressing its willful withholding. The State-law origin and absence of a negotiated bargain do not erase the obligation's economic payment character.

The strongest objection treats the default as a local family failure with a geographical label. Lopez rejects deriving federal power from remote chains through poverty, welfare expense, crime or productivity. The Court relies on none. Harris and Bishop/Stokes examine the actual economic vehicle-taking class and separately preserve the enacted vehicle element; Hale addresses possession integral to direct market regulation. They require attention to the actual object and relation, not an automatic commerce label for every debt or object with interstate history. The present due cross-border payment supplies that relation independently.

Lopez also forbids rewriting a statute to supply a missing element. No flight, travel, voluntary State crossing, bank wire, particular instrument or motive to evade is added here. The Court decides no statute lacking the different-state condition and no unrelated obligation bearing only an incidental geographical feature. It makes no finding of deliberate evasion or ability to pay.

##### II. Direct regulation of these private obligors neither commandeers a State nor issues a domestic-relations decree

**Holding and operative rule:** Section 228's direct regulation of the private obligor does not compel State administration, and the limited domestic-relations exception does not bar these federal prosecutions. The existing operative support order supplies a predicate; federal courts may apply the offense's elements and lawful defenses but may not create or modify that obligation, custody, parentage or domestic status.

**Authority:** The common nine-Justice coalition joins Part II in full.

**Controlling explanation:** New York v. United States distinguishes valid direct private regulation from compelled State responsibility. Section 228 commands no State legislature, court or executive officer to legislate, enforce the debt, investigate for federal officials, alter an order or assume the obligor's liability. Printz's qualified executive-assistance rule concerns a different means of implementation. This prosecution requires no approval of compulsory State assistance and presents no analogous fiscal question. The absence of commandeering alone supplies no commerce power; Part I independently supplies it.

Ankenbrandt v. Richards confines the statutory diversity exception to issuance of divorce, alimony and child-custody decrees, rather than imposing a general Article III exclusion for all matters involving families. This federal criminal proceeding issues no such decree. The State-law origin of the debt therefore neither defeats the established federal power nor transfers family-law authority to the federal tribunal. The Court does not recalculate support, determine a modification or prescribe State enforcement machinery. A cognizable challenge to whether the predicate order exists and remains operative is not foreclosed. Hypothetical interference with a different State proceeding is not decided.

##### III. Both prosecutions remain confined to post-enactment failures and proof of every element

**Holding and operative rule:** Federal conviction and punishment must rest on willful failures after §228's October 25, 1992 enactment, with every applicable element proved beyond a reasonable doubt. Earlier arrears may establish lawful background or past-due status, but a completed pre-enactment failure cannot itself constitute the federal offense.

**Authority:** The common nine-Justice coalition joins Part III in full.

**Controlling explanation:** Mussari's alleged period starts November 1, 1988, and Schroeder's February 1, 1992. Neither indictment's earlier starting date enlarges the enacted offense. The Ex Post Facto Clause independently prohibits punishment for conduct completed before enactment. Landgraf and Rivers reinforce attention to the legal consequences attached to completed conduct; their distinct civil approaches do not replace that criminal prohibition or require agreement on every earlier temporal rationale.

The constitutional ruling establishes neither defendant's willfulness, capacity to pay, qualifying fixed amount, required unpaid duration, different-state residence for the necessary period, or any sentencing fact. Ability-related defenses recognized by law and other lawful defenses remain available. Each existing prosecution returns for ordinary proceedings within its charges and applicable statutory, temporal and procedural limits. No new allegation, amended indictment, offense period, conviction or special trial instruction beyond this legal boundary is directed. The Court adopts no comprehensive continuing-offense theory to eliminate a separate proof or notice question.

##### IV. Each appellate trial remand stands; any restitution remains a separate conditional issue

**Holding and operative rule:** The Ninth Circuit's judgment reversing each district-court indictment dismissal and remanding each prosecution is affirmed, subject to the post-enactment limit and ordinary proof requirements. Section 228(c) requires restitution under §3663 upon conviction equal to the past-due obligation existing at sentencing; this pretrial decision fixes no amount and does not decide the precise lawful treatment of older arrears in such an order.

**Authority:** The common nine-Justice coalition joins Part IV and both disposition components in full.

**Controlling explanation:** Sustaining the presented constitutional basis for prosecution does not decide guilt or sentencing. The statutory first-offense exposure is a fine, imprisonment up to six months, or both; a subsequent offense permits a fine, imprisonment up to two years, or both. No prior offense or sentence is found here. Restitution's separate command is conditional on conviction. The rule against punishing a completed pre-enactment omission does not automatically exclude every older arrear from a later restitution calculation; nor does the sentencing-balance language automatically approve inclusion without the separate statutory and constitutional inquiry. Both questions remain for any proceeding in which they actually arise. Neither dismissal is restored. The Court orders no detention, conviction, restitution award, compensation proceeding, State-order revision or compulsory State administrative act.

#### Precedent Treatment

- United States v. Lopez retains its rejection of the remote downstream-effects chain for stand-alone school-zone possession and its prohibition on supplying a missing statutory commerce element. It is distinguished by §228's direct interstate payment object.
- United States v. Harris and Bishop/Stokes preserve their actual economic vehicle-taking ground and proof of the enacted vehicle nexus. Their result is not converted into an automatic instrumentality rule or a holding about every debt.
- United States v. Hale preserves its integral-market ground and rejection of a universal transaction-specific nexus requirement; the present payment relation must independently support federal power.
- New York v. United States preserves the distinction between direct private regulation within enumerated power and compulsory State responsibility.
- Printz/Mack's qualified source-and-function rule and confined fiscal mandate concern compelled public administration. They supply neither the commerce premise nor a fiscal remand for these private obligations; no compensation rule is adopted.
- Ankenbrandt v. Richards preserves the statutory diversity-decree exception and rejects a general Article III family-law exclusion. Federal enforcement here issues no domestic-relations decree.
- Landgraf and Rivers retain their civil temporal rules at their own scope; the independent Ex Post Facto prohibition controls completed pre-enactment criminal conduct. No earlier decision is overruled.

#### Law After Decision

Section 228 may directly protect the legally fixed payment obligation owed across State lines on the narrow ground stated. Its actual elements remain necessary; no generalized economic-effects rationale, universal debt rule or judicially added travel requirement governs. State authority to establish and modify the underlying support duty remains intact. The criminal offense-date boundary and any eventual treatment of older arrears in restitution remain distinct.

### 1997-09-08 — Faragher v. City of Boca Raton; Eleventh Circuit No. 94-4878; no separate Supreme Court docket supplied; OT1996, chunk 13.

Authority: [Record](../records/Faragher_v_City_of_Boca_Raton_merits_1997-09-08.md).

#### Holdings

##### I. Actual delegated authority can establish responsibility without higher-management notice

**Holding and operative rule:** Actual delegated supervisory authority materially aiding creation or maintenance of an actionable hostile environment supplies an independent ground for employer responsibility under Title VII; the plaintiff must establish that connection. Supervisory rank or workplace proximity alone is insufficient; higher-management notice, an express threat, a completed personnel decision and tangible economic loss are not invariably required.

**Authority:** Justice Breyer's Part I is joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg. Those nine directly support this rule. The eight Associates join Parts II–IV and the judgment in full; that common eight-Justice coalition controls the remaining holdings.

**Controlling explanation:** Title VII protects employment conditions and includes an employer's agent in its definition. Meritor directs an agency inquiry while rejecting both automatic responsibility for every supervisor's act and automatic immunity without management notice. Andrade supplies the required actual-power connection, and Oncale applies it while preserving discriminatory causation, an actionable environment and attribution as separate predicates.

Delegated control over daily working conditions may materially aid the discriminatory conditions even when the misconduct serves a personal purpose and violates employer policy. An employer's prohibition of harassment therefore does not alone answer whether its actual delegation aided the wrong. But employment merely providing an opportunity to encounter the plaintiff is not enough. The plaintiff must prove the connection.

Ordinary scope of employment, apparent authority and employer negligence remain distinct routes. Higher-management knowledge matters to negligence without becoming an additional element of proved actual-authority attribution. Harris and DeAngelis govern the separate contextual hostile-environment threshold; proof meeting that threshold does not itself establish agency or constructive notice. The Court applies the actual-authority route here and leaves the alternative routes undecided.

##### II. The supported operational findings establish the required connection here

**Holding and operative rule:** The established allocation and exercise of assignments, discipline, daily duties and supervision in this work unit materially aided maintenance of its accepted hostile conditions. These supported bench findings establish the actual-authority ground without a new threat, fear or employment-penalty finding, and do not require a further attribution proceeding.

**Authority:** The common eight-Justice coalition joins Part II. Chief Justice Stone-Zsela does not join this application.

**Controlling explanation:** Terry controlled assignments, reprimands and personnel-file discipline and selected recruits subject to higher approval. Silverman controlled daily duties, assignments and fitness routines. Their powers actually governed the working conditions of a geographically separated unit organized through their command. The district court's agency determination rested on those powers and the workplace structure, independently of its disputed constructive-notice ground.

This was more than supervisory capacity accompanied by an opportunity for misconduct. The operative control of Faragher's daily duties and on-site working conditions supplied the authority through which these supervisors maintained the repeated abusive environment. Remoteness and ineffective policy communication reinforce that practical structure; neither becomes a required element for every future plaintiff or a substitute for actual aid. The Court attributes this established course of hostile working conditions, not every personal act of every supervisor.

Historical facts receive clear-error review; their legal significance receives independent review. The Court adds no finding that Faragher feared discharge, received an order to submit, faced a particular threat, lost wages or suffered an employment penalty. Making a firing threat or completed adverse decision indispensable would restore the restriction Andrade rejects.

The strongest remand objection is that a list of powers shows only capacity and that the trial's agency label did not expressly distinguish facilitation from rank. The supported findings go further: they describe the actual organization and exercise of control over the conditions in which the established abuse was maintained. Their legal consequence can be decided without inventing another historical fact. Meritor's unresolved harassment findings and Andrade's unresolved verdict, instruction and sufficiency questions warranted their own remands; neither requires a new proceeding on this adequate bench record. Whether constructive notice or Gordon's knowledge independently establishes liability is unnecessary to decide.

##### III. This ineffective-policy contention does not defeat liability; a general defense remains open

**Holding and operative rule:** In this case, the combination of a policy not communicated to the relevant workforce, failure to complain to distant higher management and correction after another employee's eventual report does not defeat the proved authority-aided liability. The Court leaves open whether genuinely effective protection and unreasonable employee nonuse could establish a complete defense, including its elements, burden, relationship to tangible employment action and any distinct limitation on particular relief.

**Authority:** The common eight-Justice coalition joins Part III. Chief Justice Stone-Zsela agrees separately that an undistributed policy does not establish unreasonable nonuse and that later correction does not erase earlier attributable misconduct, but would reject the proposed complete defense rather than reserve it.

**Controlling explanation:** Meritor does not make a paper grievance policy and noncomplaint conclusive. An uncommunicated procedure does not establish available protection that an employee unreasonably declined. Prompt action after eventual notice matters to the adequacy of that response; it does not establish effective protection during the earlier authority-aided environment or retroactively erase that conduct.

The grant permits consideration of a complete defense, and effective prevention and reasonable avoidance present serious interests. But Andrade already supplies a plaintiff-proved actual-aid limitation, and the City's present contention fails without deciding how genuinely effective measures would affect responsibility. The Court neither adopts a new burden-shifting formula nor rejects every possible complete defense. Nor does it decide a tangible-action exception or a general duty to complain.

No finding is made that no alternative official could ever have been approached, that the policy contained a particular promise, or that Faragher held an unproved belief. Questions about alternative reporting and whether dissemination would have exposed the misconduct belong to their proper agency, negligence or remedial inquiries; they need not be resolved against the City to sustain this independent ground. Failure to disseminate a policy alone does not prove every negligence element or create a freestanding statutory publication duty. Effective procedures, knowledge, correction and avoidable loss retain their possible legal significance where their actual predicates are presented.

##### IV. The existing nominal judgment is reinstated within the grant's limits

**Holding and operative rule:** The appellate judgment is reversed only insofar as it reversed Faragher's Title VII judgment against the City, and the case is remanded for reinstatement of the existing one-dollar judgment without a new merits trial or further agency findings. No individual or state-law award, remaining appellate disposition, fee entitlement or additional remedy is adjudicated.

**Authority:** The common eight-Justice coalition joins Part IV and this mandate. Chief Justice Stone-Zsela instead supports the distinct conditional remand described in his separate writing.

**Controlling explanation:** The sufficient actual-authority ground supports the existing judgment independently of constructive notice, imputation of Gordon's knowledge, ordinary employment scope or apparent authority. Those alternatives remain undecided; a defect in an unnecessary alternative does not require an exploratory proceeding on the sufficient ground.

Landgraf bars attaching the 1991 Act's new §102 compensatory and punitive liabilities to this 1985–1990 conduct; its dependent jury provision creates no new jury right here. Restoration of nominal relief does not enlarge that remedy. The separate $10,000 §1983 judgment against Terry and Silverman and $500 battery punitive award against Terry remain outside the grant, along with other state claims and remaining appellate dispositions.

Farrar separates enforceable nominal relief from the reasonable fee amount under §1988. That distinct statute supplies only a limited analogy; any Title VII fee question requires its own entitlement and reasonableness analysis. The Court fixes no fee, new damages, prospective injunction, constructive-discharge finding or employment reinstatement. The appellate remand implements the existing one-dollar judgment and sets no special deadline or retained proceeding.

#### Precedent Treatment

- Meritor Savings Bank v. Vinson preserves agency-based attribution, the rejection of automatic liability for every supervisor's conduct, and the rejection of a conclusive paper-policy/noncomplaint defense. Its unresolved findings do not require a new trial on this supported record; no comprehensive defense is supplied by its reservation.
- Andrade v. Mayfair Management applies its actual-delegated-authority/material-aid rule, including the plaintiff's connection requirement and rejection of categorical management-notice or tangible-action prerequisites. Its distinct Rule 50 remand does not require renewed factfinding here; its reservation of general defenses remains open.
- Oncale v. Sundowner Offshore Services applies its reaffirmation of Andrade and preserves separate sex-causation, hostile-environment and attribution predicates. Its allegation-stage remand supplies no contrary command for these tried findings.
- Harris v. Forklift Systems retains the contextual objective-and-subjective hostile-environment inquiry without mandatory psychological or economic injury. It does not establish employer attribution or constructive notice merely from severity.
- DeAngelis v. El Paso Municipal Police Officers' Association preserves its application of that contextual threshold without extra injury or hierarchy prerequisites. Its distinct newsletter record does not resolve the present attribution inquiry.
- Landgraf v. USI Film Products preserves the unavailability of new §102 damages for this pre-enactment conduct and the dependent jury limit. No new damages or jury entitlement is created.
- Farrar v. Hobby retains the distinction between enforceable nominal relief and a reasonable fee amount under §1988. It does not decide the separate Title VII fee question. No earlier decision is overruled.

#### Law After Decision

The actual-authority route remains a fact-dependent ground separate from negligence, apparent authority and ordinary employment scope. Existing findings of the operational control that materially aided these hostile conditions suffice for the nominal City judgment. A paper policy, noncomplaint to higher management and eventual correction supply no defense on this record. The Court adopts neither a general preventive-care/nonuse defense nor a rule forbidding every such defense; its elements, burden, tangible-action relationship and any distinct remedial limitation remain open. No title-based liability, automatic knowledge imputation or general complaint duty follows.

### 1997-09-15 — Harrison v. Eddy Potash, Inc.; Tenth Circuit Nos. 96-2045 and 96-2065; 112 F.3d 1437; no separate Supreme Court docket supplied.

Authority: [Record](../records/Harrison_v_Eddy_Potash_Inc_merits_1997-09-15.md).

#### Holdings

##### I. Material aid from actual delegated power does not require alter-ego rank

**Holding and operative rule:** An employer may be responsible under Title VII when actual delegated supervisory power materially aids creation or maintenance of an actionable hostile environment; the plaintiff must prove that connection by a preponderance of the evidence. Hiring or firing authority, alter-ego identity, higher-management notice, an express threat, a completed personnel action and tangible economic loss are not invariably required, while rank, employment or workplace proximity alone is insufficient.

**Authority:** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela's opinion of the Court, Parts I–V, has all nine direct joins: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. This common coalition controls all five holdings and the mandate.

**Controlling explanation:** Title VII's inclusion of an employer's agents and Meritor require an actual agency inquiry, distinct from ordinary employment scope and negligence. Andrade, Oncale and Faragher establish the plaintiff-proved connection between delegated authority and the unlawful conditions. Personal purpose or violation of a prohibition does not alone negate that connection; permission to harass is not its prerequisite.

Harrison's account describes Brown using work orders to move her away from her station or buddy into isolated areas, where misconduct allegedly followed. Control over where, with whom and on what task she worked could materially aid abuse even without top-management powers. That evidence supports submission of the route; the Court does not find every incident proved. Conversely, impressive powers do not establish that they aided any particular wrong.

The agency definition required managerial control making Brown the employer's alter ego. Its reference to control over employment conditions did not remove that categorical restriction. Meritor rejects the opposite status-alone rule too, so rejection of Harrison's overbroad proposed formulations was proper. She was entitled to an accurate instruction on a supported route, not every requested sentence.

An actionable environment and sex-based causation remain separate. Harris requires conditions sufficiently severe or pervasive, in all the circumstances, to be objectively hostile or abusive and actually perceived as abusive. Frequency, severity, physical threat or humiliation and interference with work inform that inquiry; none is indispensable, and psychological injury, treatment and lost productivity are not prerequisites. Oncale preserves proof that the conditions were imposed because of sex. Grave misconduct alone supplies neither causation nor employer attribution.

##### II. The charge prejudicially withheld the supported actual-authority route

**Holding and operative rule:** Considered as a whole against this record, the preserved charge was prejudicially incomplete because it made apparent authority and reasonable reliance cumulative requirements, imposed an alter-ego barrier and omitted the supported actual-authority/material-aid route. If a distinct apparent-authority theory is properly submitted, it requires reasonable belief traceable to the employer's words or conduct and reasonable reliance on that appearance, not merely the supervisor's claimed power; that alternative is not a condition of actual-authority attribution.

**Authority:** All nine Justices join Part II. The actual-authority omission independently suffices for affirmance of the instructional reversal; factual sufficiency of apparent authority is not decided.

**Controlling explanation:** The principal charge was given over objection, and the requested instructions presented the aid issue as well as overbroad status-based theories. Independent review of the whole charge, with prejudice required, differs from reviewing the choice of a particular requested instruction for abuse of discretion. Neither inquiry requires verbatim use of an inaccurate proposal.

The charge's reference to authority otherwise than apparently did not explain material aid or remove the mandatory apparent-authority and reliance elements. Brown's daily control and lack of top-management status made those barriers consequential. Work-order evidence concretely supported the omitted route. A possible jury rejection of another Title VII element does not establish that this general employer verdict rested on an independent, correctly decided ground; no special finding supplies that conclusion. Nor does the separate tort verdict against Brown establish the statutory elements against Potash. This is a record-specific prejudice determination, not automatic reversal for any agency error.

Restatement §27 supplies the limited principal-manifestation clarification. Faragher left apparent authority undecided; its separate observations are not a Court holding. An employee's knowledge of a supervisor's assertion is not a substitute for manifestations attributable to the employer. Knowledge that harassment is forbidden does not erase actual command power. An effectively implemented policy may bear on a properly framed apparent-authority inquiry, but the Court decides neither that route's factual sufficiency nor that ignorance of policy alone establishes it. It does not adopt every apparent-authority formulation below or extend Faragher's actual-delegation rule to every claimed apparent power.

##### III. Policy and response do not cure the omitted route; a general complete defense remains open

**Holding and operative rule:** A prohibition of harassment and correction after notice do not themselves negate earlier material aid from actual delegated power or cure the prejudicially incomplete charge. The Court preserves Faragher's reservation concerning a general complete defense based on genuinely effective prevention and unreasonable employee nonuse, including its elements, burden, relation to tangible employment action and any distinct limitation on relief.

**Authority:** All nine Justices join Part III, including its limited reservation of the Court's general complete-defense question. No complete defense is adopted or supplied to Potash.

**Controlling explanation:** Faragher rejected the ineffective-policy contention on its own proved record while adopting neither a general defense nor categorical rejection of every such defense. Harrison requires her own policy chronology. She discovered a posted policy after some incidents, and it was absent from her new-hire materials. Those facts establish neither universal ignorance nor that every reporting route was unavailable, nonuse was unreasonable or every remedial step was inadequate.

After her July report, Potash investigated, promised lost-time compensation and treatment, changed her crew, reprimanded Brown, placed him on permanent probation for recurrence and restricted contact. Those measures retain their potential relevance to employer care, response and relief; they do not retroactively remove earlier actual aid. Failed dissemination alone is not negligence per se. The investigator's acceptance of Harrison's unwilling participation alongside Brown's asserted perception of consent is not a judicial finding that the conduct was welcome; Meritor distinguishes unwelcome conduct from apparently voluntary participation.

The different policy facts permit their proper consideration, but establish no complete defense here. The charge was not an accurate, separately justified instruction on an established defense. Faragher's reservation does not expand the granted or preserved issues, create a reporting duty or supply an appellate finding against Harrison. Appropriate apparent-authority, negligence and remedial inquiries remain distinct. No omnibus policy immunity, new burden-shifting formula or freestanding policy-publication duty is adopted.

##### IV. This appellate record establishes no contractual bar to the independent Title VII action

**Holding and operative rule:** A contractual grievance assertion does not remove federal subject-matter jurisdiction over an independent Title VII claim. Potash cannot obtain dismissal for nonexhaustion on this appellate record, which includes neither its CBA nor the district court's exhaustion ruling and identifies no agreement covering arbitration of statutory claims or delegation of the antecedent question.

**Authority:** All nine Justices join Part IV and affirmance of the rejection of the employer's cross-appeal.

**Controlling explanation:** Gardner-Denver preserves independent Title VII rights despite contractual grievance arbitration. Gilmer enforces an actual agreement to arbitrate the statutory ADEA claim; it does not supply a missing agreement here or overrule the contractual/statutory distinction. First Options requires courts independently to determine agreement and clear, unmistakable delegation under applicable contract law. A bargaining relationship or asserted grievance process proves neither statutory scope nor delegation. Its conditional rule for review after actual delegation is not reached.

The appellate opinion's two footnotes report the CBA and order omissions and that Potash's brief did not identify statutory arbitration. These are actual limits of its appellate presentation, not a finding that no contract ever existed or a fabricated waiver. The strongest enforcement argument recognizes that a proven forum agreement can create duties without extinguishing substantive rights; it still requires the agreement this record does not establish.

Livadas and Hawaiian Airlines require attention to the actual source of a right and whether disputed contract interpretation is necessary. Whether sex-based conditions and delegated power meet Title VII's elements does not require such interpretation here. Their distinct preemption holdings do not establish immunity from every arbitration agreement. The Court declines the lower court's blanket CBA/FAA rationale. Gilmer reserved the general employment-contract exclusion; that question and the validity of every explicit collective statutory-arbitration agreement remain unresolved. No contract-recovery or new exhaustion proceeding is ordered merely to rescue the unsupported cross-appeal.

##### V. Both appellate results stand, with liability and relief for proper further proceedings

**Holding and operative rule:** The Tenth Circuit's reversal of Potash's Title VII verdict and remand in No. 96-2045, and its rejection of Potash's cross-appeal in No. 96-2065, are affirmed. The remand contemplates a new Title VII trial under corrected instructions, subject to lawful resolution of genuinely preserved independent grounds; if the surviving claim is submitted to a jury, the supported actual-authority route must be accurately instructed, with the prejudicial error already resolved.

**Authority:** All nine Justices join Part V and the common further-proceedings mandate.

**Controlling explanation:** No second appellate reconsideration of the same prejudice question is required. The lower opinion identifies the preserved omission, supporting evidence and resulting prejudice; Faragher's intervening rule now governs directly. Its restoration of a nominal judgment on supported bench findings and an accepted environment does not transfer findings to Harrison's jury case. Brown's separate $102,500 compensatory and $40,000 punitive tort awards concern a different defendant and different elements; they remain undisturbed and do not become an award against Potash.

The 1993 incidents postdate November 21, 1991, so Landgraf's temporal bar does not confine Harrison to Faragher's one-dollar remedy. This establishes no entitlement or amount. Section 102 compensation remains distinct from §706(g) relief and excludes backpay, interest on backpay and other relief authorized by §706(g). Punitive relief requires malice or reckless indifference to federally protected rights; no such finding is made. When available §102 compensatory or punitive damages are sought, either party may demand a jury, which must not be told the statutory monetary caps. No cap calculation is made here. Ordinary protection against duplicate compensation applies.

The Court awards no damages, fees, reinstatement or other new relief and adjudicates no new termination or constructive-discharge claim. Independent fee requirements remain for a properly presented collateral issue. The preserved defenses and remaining statutory elements are not displaced by reversal of a defective charge.

#### Precedent Treatment

- Meritor supplies agency analysis, preserves the distinction between unwelcome conduct and voluntary participation, and rejects automatic supervisor liability and conclusive paper-policy immunity.
- Andrade supplies the actual-delegation/material-aid route and its connection requirement; its separate Rule 50 remand does not require another appellate prejudice proceeding here.
- Oncale preserves sex causation, actionable conditions and attribution as separate predicates, and applies Andrade without a title-only rule.
- Faragher supplies the actual-authority rule and preserves the general-defense reservation. Its bench findings, nominal restoration and pre-1991 remedy setting are distinguished; its apparent-authority alternative remains undecided.
- Harris supplies the contextual objective-and-subjective severe-or-pervasive standard without injury or productivity prerequisites. DeAngelis preserves that standard without adding hierarchy, physical advance or work-loss requirements. Neither establishes attribution from severity alone.
- Gardner-Denver preserves the independent Title VII right despite contractual grievance arbitration. Gilmer enforces an actual statutory-arbitration agreement without supplying absent terms or deciding the general FAA employment-contract exclusion.
- First Options requires antecedent agreement and clear, unmistakable delegation; its conditional post-delegation review rule is not reached.
- Livadas and Hawaiian Airlines preserve independent rights where disputed contract interpretation is unnecessary. Their preemption holdings do not decide every statutory-arbitration agreement.
- Landgraf's pre-enactment restriction does not impose a nominal-only remedy for 1993 conduct. Its distinct §102 compensation, punitive and jury conditions remain applicable. No earlier decision is overruled.

#### Law After Decision

The actual-authority route must be available when concrete evidence supports material aid from delegated work power, without mandatory alter-ego status or apparent-authority reliance. This charge prejudicially excluded that route. Policy and response retain their proper, fact-dependent roles; the general complete-defense question remains open. This unsupported contractual-exhaustion assertion does not bar the independent statutory action, but no universal CBA/FAA or collective statutory-arbitration rule follows. Employer liability and relief remain for the proper further proceedings.

## 4. Material Published Noncontrolling Positions

### 1996-11-04 — California v. Roy, No. 95-2025; October Term 1996, chunk 1.

**Chief Justice Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and in the judgment; no joins.** He joins Part II and supports vacatur and remand because the Ninth Circuit's necessity formulation does not replace the whole-record Chapman inquiry required for the preserved personal-intent claim. Gaudin protects jury determination of elements without making every omission structural; Sullivan's destruction of the reasonable-doubt verdict differs from this assessable omission. O'Neal puts on the State the burden to establish beyond a reasonable doubt that the violation did not contribute to the verdict. He would neither supply intent himself, shift the burden to Roy nor demand innocence. If a properly available violation fails the State's showing, relief for the affected convictions must permit a reasonable retrial opportunity. Preservation, exhaustion, independent habeas requirements and statutory transition remain separate. He makes no final harmlessness finding and sets no retrial deadline. He does not join Parts I or III's additional reasoning.

**Justice Stevens, concurring in part and dissenting in part; no joins.** He joins Parts I and II but would affirm the habeas-relief judgment on this record. His Rose concurrence and his agreement with Yates require rigorous inquiry into the error's contribution to the actual verdict. The distinct omitted purpose, the supported inference of companion assistance without a robbery purpose, the disputed advance-plan account and the absence of an established independent purpose finding prevent the State from proving harmlessness beyond a reasonable doubt. This does not establish that every defense assertion is true or that the jury rejected all of Hudspeth's testimony. Stevens accepts that the Ninth Circuit's general necessary-findings formula is too broad; he does not adopt it as the exclusive rule for every omission. A proper actual-contribution inquiry nevertheless supports the judgment already reached. No identified unfinished material task justifies another remand merely to repeat an adverse Chapman determination. He would leave conditional relief for the two Mannix convictions in place, with a reasonable retrial opportunity and no immediate unconditional release.

**Justice Scalia, concurring in part and dissenting in part, joined by Justice Ginsburg.** They join Parts I and II but would affirm. For this omitted-purpose error, harmlessness requires that the jury's other determinations effectively embrace Roy's required purpose, or that the evidence and findings establish that the jury could not have reached what it did find without also finding that purpose. The State must establish that connection beyond a reasonable doubt. Carella's separate opinion and Scalia's Yates opinion explain why independent appellate certainty that a properly instructed jury would convict cannot replace the jury's actual findings; Sullivan and Gaudin preserve the jury's constitutional role. Whole-record review identifies what the actual verdict embraces; it does not authorize an appellate substitute verdict.

Knowledge and assistance do not necessarily establish purpose. Neither the Clark findings nor general capacity answers the missing Mannix purpose. The conditional nonkiller clause, the distinction between intentional assistance to first-degree murder and purpose to facilitate robbery, the robbery-related purpose of the killing, and the cross-reference to deficient aiding instructions prevent treating the special circumstances as an established equivalent finding. The asserted preservation objection does not itself supply forfeiture, and the record does not identify an unresolved genuine finding question requiring another remand. A valid equivalent finding could make an omission harmless, so their rule is not automatic structural reversal. They would affirm conditional relief only for the two Mannix convictions, allowing a reasonable retrial period. They adopt no innocence prerequisite or discretionary-habeas rule, and Ginsburg joins no such proposition.

### 1996-11-06 — Lopez v. Monterey County; No. 95-1201

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela concurs in the Court's entire opinion and judgment. He also concludes that South Carolina v. Katzenbach, which sustains the Act's coverage and preclearance machinery, and City of Rome, which sustains its operation against covered governmental units, foreclose the facial constitutional objection to the County's operative designation. This is distinct from the Court's statutory bar on collateral retrial of the coverage findings. He further states that the wholly judicial exception does not apply when a court adopts material electoral policy choices proposed, required or previously selected by the County or the State. Necessity and independent remedial authority must support any genuinely court-formulated temporary plan; he selects no plan and decides no purpose or effect question. No other Justice joins these additional formulations.

### 1996-11-18 — Ohio v. Robinette; No. 95-891

**Chief Justice Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** He would vacate the Ohio judgment and remand. He joins the no-script rule, the objective continued-seizure inquiry, and the Court's requirements to examine voluntariness and any necessary causal relationship to unlawful detention. A State cannot convert uninterrupted official restraint into consent merely by describing it as a request. Immediate questioning, documents, tone, positioning and the absence of an objective release signal bear on whether the motorist remained seized and whether the choice was real. A clear warning is strong evidence and may be required by state law or policy. He reaches no final admissibility result and preserves suppression where the applicable inquiries fail. He agrees to federal review and to setting aside the motive-based exit-order ground without adding a reason on those components; his chosen formal disposition remains vacatur, not reversal.

**Justice Ginsburg, concurring in the judgment.** She accepts federal review under governing Long despite her earlier preference in Evans for a different jurisdictional presumption. The Ohio opinion's interwoven analysis supplies no clearly independent state basis. She agrees that federal law requires no universal release script and that actual consent must be assessed under the total circumstances. Her agreement does not decide that Robinette's search was valid or that no detention continued. She emphasizes that Ohio may use its own Constitution to require a clear warning, provided it rests the rule on an independent state ground. Federal correction of this judgment does not displace that authority. She does not join Stevens's conclusion that this record already requires suppression.

**Justice Stevens, dissenting.** He accepts review and rejects an indispensable federal warning formula, but would affirm suppression on the actual encounter. His Bostick dissent's attention to the practical force of police authority, together with Royer and Brown's separation of consent from unlawful detention, leads him to treat the continued official direction after completion of traffic business as restraint requiring an independent justification. The deputy's question before departure continued that restraint; no separate suspicion or intervening circumstance supplies a lawful extension or breaks the connection to consent. Returning the license and Robinette's initial sense of freedom do not decide the effect of the subsequent direction. The deputy's courtesy, lack of a drawn weapon and Robinette's education bear on voluntariness, but furnish no intervening break from the detention. Stevens does not invalidate the initial stop or a lawful exit order because of hidden motive, and he proposes no automatic suppression rule after every illegality. His disagreement is with the Court's refusal to affirm suppression on this record, not with Ohio's freedom to require warnings under independent state law.

### 1996-11-25 — Hopwood v. Texas; Fifth Circuit No. 94-50664, 78 F.3d 932; no invented Supreme Court docket; OT1996, chunk 1, matter 6.

**Kennedy, concurring in part and concurring in the judgment.** Kennedy joins Parts I, III and IV–V but does not join Part II. He would assume a potentially compelling educational interest and invalidate the actual process for inadequate tailoring. Croson supports rigorous application without an unnecessary categorical prohibition; his Metro reasoning rejects assigning a contribution to an applicant merely from racial identity. The combination of different thresholds and separate decision rules remains unjustified despite individual exceptions within each track. He agrees that the appellate diversity prohibition must be removed from this remand but reserves the affirmative compelling-interest question. He neither requires identical numerical evaluation in every future program nor approves the later design.

**Scalia, concurring in part and dissenting in part; Thomas joins Section A.** Section A rejects nonremedial racial preferences as a justification for burdening an individual applicant. The equal-protection right belongs to the person, and educational aims do not turn racial ancestry into an entitlement or establish that group membership predicts educational contribution. The actual five-Justice Bakke Part V-C proposition is acknowledged; these Justices would expressly disapprove it to the extent it authorizes nonremedial preferences. They therefore dissent from vacating the diversity prohibition and from Part II, while joining the narrow invalidity holding and the individual causation/remedy provisions. They accept the same-decision allocation and preponderance requirement, but their substantive view excludes nonremedial preferences from the lawful counterfactual. Individual experiences may still be considered under lawful nonracial criteria.

In Section B, which Thomas does not join, Scalia declines the broader institutional rule and further remedial inquiry in Part III. Even assuming a broader responsible unit, the record does not establish that these preferences were necessary to remove a traceable barrier. He recognizes Fordice as existing authority and does not seek to overrule it, but would resolve this offered defense without the additional remand inquiry. Thomas instead joins Part III’s bounded recognition of the State’s duty; that join does not equate enrollment targets with removal of inherited barriers. Neither Justice supports a new injunction or punitive award, treats benevolent purpose as eliminating statutory intent, or deems every constitutionally valid remedial act forbidden merely because it considers race.

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and concurring in the judgment.** The Chief Justice joins Parts I–III, IV-D and V. He agrees with the individual-relief remand and punitive denial, without joining Parts IV-A–C. He would assess claimed individualization by actual operation: the order of decisions, thresholds, separate review, numerical aims, discretion, beneficiary categories, whether assumptions can genuinely be rebutted, and workable alternatives. A small formal weight for race is no answer when it determines outcomes near the admission threshold. Conversely, a program lacking quotas, separate tracks and numerical aims is not invalid merely because race is one consideration among several; no particular such program is approved. The combined 1992 design made race decisive across broad categories without the supported necessity and individualized fit he requires.

He understands a permissible educational objective to require concrete benefits from meaningful institutional inclusion, an explanation of the mechanism connecting the classification to those benefits, and attention to actual burdens. Racial arithmetic, generalized societal discrimination, reputation, hostility outside the institution, and assumptions that identity predicts viewpoint cannot substitute for that showing. For corrective measures he additionally requires objective evidence of the persisting effect, scope fitted to it, meaningful continuing opportunity for others, respect for legally protected existing interests, and termination when the basis ends. The State bears its justification burden. These additional formulations are his separate grounds, not additions to the Court’s controlling rule.

His causation position distinguishes the established unequal process from a claimed lost seat or monetary loss. A defendant may defeat admission-related compensation by proving that a specified lawful process would have produced the same denial, without erasing the violation. He would preserve nominal and declaratory recognition and fee-free lawful consideration if practically available, leaving the proper cause, defendant, immunity and precise relief for determination below. He agrees with the disposition of the separate statutory-intent component without adopting the Court’s statutory rationale.

### 1996-12-02 — Tyler Murray v. Montrose County School District RE-1J; Tenth Circuit Nos. 93-1466 and 93-1474; no Supreme Court docket assigned.

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela dissents. He would affirm the Tenth Circuit and reach the preserved geographic legal question while treating the individualized former-placement and later-progress disputes as moot. In his view, IDEA's preference for education with nondisabled children is distinct from geographic proximity: the regulations make proximity and the neighborhood school mandatory considerations, but permit another arrangement when the individualized IEP requires it. He would reject an independent burden-shifting neighborhood-school presumption without approving convenience-based transfers, diminishing the duty to use supplementary aids, or declaring distance irrelevant. A district's assertion that its specialized program is better would not establish compliance.

He would recognize section 1415(e)(2)'s additional-evidence channel in a live dispute, including relevant subsequent progress with its temporal relevance explained, while giving due weight to the administrative proceedings without surrendering independent legal judgment. He would order no new evidence here: the aids proffer does not establish the geographic-presumption theory, the independent unexhausted aids issue is not reached, and the later IEP removes the placement/progress remedy. He declines the wider evidentiary disagreement and any ruling on Northside's factual adequacy. His proposed legal answer and affirmance do not command a majority; the Court holds the controversy moot.

### 1996-12-09 — In re Askin; Fourth Circuit No. 94-5428, 47 F.3d 100; no separate Supreme Court docket supplied; October Term 1996.

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and in the judgment; no joins.** He agrees that the former wire/electronic exclusions cover the intercepted radio segment carrying both voices and that the 1994 deletion cannot retroactively make completed surveillance unlawful. His statutory position treats the place of acquisition as controlling under the former cordless exclusion. He would affirm the lower court's complete former-Title-III noncoverage ruling for that acquired segment and does not join the Court's additional oral-coverage route. Statutory noncoverage, on his view, neither authorizes interception at another point nor determines constitutional privacy.

He joins rejection of the categorical Fourth Amendment ruling and would state a further conditional rule: absent participant consent, a willing informant or knowing exposure, a landline or cellular caller does not surrender privacy merely because the other participant uses a vulnerable cordless handset without the caller's knowledge. *Katz* protects the speaker's own private words. *White* assigns the risk that an interlocutor will reveal or transmit them; it does not eliminate privacy merely because unknown agents can independently intercept a retransmission the caller did not select or know about. This rule leaves knowing exposure, participant consent and the cordless user's own expectation distinct. The record does not establish Askin's knowledge, so he would not finally apply the rule.

He accepts *Gelbard*'s statutory just-cause principle, but proposes a separate constitutional ground for this criminal-trial setting. When compelled questions are direct fruits of unlawful acquisition of the witness's own protected calls, and no recognized exception provides a lawful basis, refusal should constitute just cause under §1826(a). Coercing this speaker's testimony through his own unlawfully intercepted words gives the exclusionary rule a direct deterrent function. Question-specific derivation, personal rights and ordinary remedial exceptions keep the proposal bounded. *Pinson* and *Wellons* do not themselves establish this extension; *Calandra*'s grand-jury rule is left intact.

He would require the lower court to determine knowledge or knowing exposure, direct derivation of each question, and any preserved independent source, attenuation, objectively reasonable good-faith reliance or other lawful basis. If the governing premises establish lack of knowledge and direct derivation from unlawful acquisition without an applicable exception, the contempt adjudication must be set aside. He grants no automatic immunity from questions and no final discharge on this record. The Court's eight-Justice opinion leaves that independent constitutional just-cause question unresolved.

### 1996-12-10 — O'Gilvie v. United States; Nos. 95-966 and 95-977

O'Connor, joined by Scalia and Thomas, would exclude the punitive receipts. The physical injury is a legal cause of the damages, even though the award's purpose is punishment. The former text says on account of personal injury, while neighboring provisions use compensation language; the dissent rejects adding a compensation-only restriction. It distinguishes Schleier's employment backpay and injury-independent willfulness payment from a traditional tort award legally dependent on the physical injury. The dissent applies both statutory conditions and does not claim every tort-type receipt is excluded. Because the children prevail on that merits ground, the dissent does not decide their limitation defense; it also regards a choice between receipt and later clearance as unnecessary once mailing is rejected. All three agree that the father's appeal is timely.

Scalia separately retains the construction expressed in his Burke concurrence: the exclusion concerns physical or mental health injuries. This wrongful-death recovery satisfies that premise, unlike the employment entitlement in Burke. He joins the shared textual and causal dissent without converting his health-injury construction into the view of O'Connor or Thomas. Both dissents are noncontrolling.

### 1996-12-16 — Greene v. Georgia; No. 96-5369

Stone-Zsela agrees that federal collateral review and state direct appellate responsibility must remain distinct. Importing the former's deference can obscure the state court's duty to correct error without legal authority. He would vacate and remand so Georgia identifies the deference, if any, supplied by state law and then decides the federal exclusion claims. His remedy does not order a new sentencing proceeding; he expresses no view on any juror's qualification, harmlessness or the ultimate capital judgment. His disagreement concerns formal relief, not the Court's source-of-review rule.

### 1996-12-16 — M.L.B. v. S.L.J.; No. 95-853

Kennedy concurs in the judgment on due process alone. Boddie, Lassiter and Santosky identify the established parental interest and the need for fair procedures without creating a civil appeal in every case. Under Mathews, the permanent loss, risk of error, practical value of a usable record and governmental burdens must be assessed in the appellate structure Mississippi actually provided. Here the unaffordable record barrier defeats that review. He supports sufficient record access and reversal, but does not join the Court's extension of Griffin's equality rationale or treat wealth as a suspect classification. This is judgment-only agreement, not an additional opinion join.

Thomas, joined by Scalia, dissents on two grounds. Due process protects the established parental interest through an adequate hearing, but Boddie's indispensable initial access does not itself compel financing an additional civil appeal. Separately, Griffin and Mayer's criminal-access exception should not be extended beyond Kras and Ortwein's ordinary civil cost-allocation rule. Permanent termination is exceptionally grave, yet seriousness and the convergence of fairness and equality do not identify an additional appellate subsidy. The dissent questions the limiting principle for other civil claims while accepting the protected parental relationship. It neither finds the termination correct nor equates poverty with unfitness, and it leaves voluntary state support available. Griffin, Mayer and Bounds are not proposed for overruling; the dissent confines its claim to nonextension here.

### 1996-12-16 — United States v. Sahhar; Ninth Circuit Nos. 94-50186 and 94-50356; separate Supreme Court docket unassigned

Stone-Zsela joins the no-sentence-cap and state-placement holdings and the affirmance. He insists that continued federal custody requires clear and convincing proof of current mental illness causing current statutory danger; historical danger, incompetence alone or the dismissed accusation cannot substitute. Counsel, a neutral hearing, practical review and genuine unconditional or conditional release must remain available. He also expressly preserves release whenever the statutory release route requires it. He does not join Part V's distinct formulation of subsection (e)'s preponderance discharge determination or its detailed procedural account, and his concurrence supplies no different universal rule for every discharge motion.

He separately concludes that the limited custody-defined class and the interests in safely winding up lawful custody, treatment and public protection are sufficiently related even under intermediate scrutiny, without choosing that tier as generally governing. He does not join the Court's separate equality formulation. Transfer efforts must be reasonable and periodically renewed; actual state acceptance ends federal retention. The remand must test current predicates and Arizona's actual response, leaving dismissal intact. His concurrence decides no freestanding enumerated-power question and authorizes neither nominal review nor permanent custody based on old findings.

### 1997-01-06 — DeAngelis v. El Paso Municipal Police Officers' Association; Fifth Circuit No. 93-8700, 51 F.3d 591; no separate Supreme Court docket supplied

**Chief Justice Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and in the judgment; no joins.** He joins the retaliation holding but rejects statutory insufficiency on hostile environment. The repeated sex-derogatory message, distribution to more than seven hundred colleagues, connections to DeAngelis, recurring comments and workplace incidents, humiliation, claimed loss of authority, promotion deterrence and refusal to identify the columnist permit a rational jury's severe-or-pervasive finding under Harris. Physical threats, supervisory power, reduced performance and the written medium are not statutory barriers. He therefore reaches the preserved expressive defense.

In his view, this award punishes protected editorial opinion or satire solely for its sex-derogatory viewpoint. Such civil liability is content based and is not narrowly tailored here to the compelling interest in eradicating sex discrimination. The publication itself is the independently asserted wrong; the record supplies no separate discriminatory employment act, true threat, authority-backed directive or denial of employment or associational rights to which the expression is integral or evidentiary. Hurley preserves the expressive inquiry, and Mitchell distinguishes punishment of protected belief from use of expression to establish an independently unlawful act. He would prohibit Title VII damages resting solely on such protected opinion or satire, while preserving liability for discriminatory decisions, quid pro quo demands, true threats, authority-backed directives and expression integral to or used as evidence of independently unlawful employment conduct. His rule is confined to this expressive application and does not declare that speech cannot itself be workplace harassment. That constitutional ground alone supports his hostile-environment affirmance. On retaliation, he finds no material employment or membership disadvantage caused by the complaint and leaves stronger threats, harassment and public-shaming cases open.

**Justice Stevens, concurring in part and dissenting in part, joined by Justice Ginsburg.** They join Part II but would reverse the hostile-environment portion and remand. Harris protects disadvantageous conditions without proof of lost output. The lower opinion's reliance on destroyed opportunity, palpable performance deterioration, missing advances and absence of a superior harasser materially narrowed its review of the jury verdict. Its correct abstract recitation of Harris and the substantial contrary contextual evidence do not cure that error. Repeated sex-based attacks, broad circulation, mocking, humiliation and alleged impairment of command warrant review without those added thresholds. Ginsburg's Harris explanation makes professional disadvantage relevant without measurable productivity loss. They find a review error, not liability as a matter of law. Mitchell and Hurley keep the preserved expressive defense distinct; it and any remaining properly preserved grounds must be resolved before liability could stand. They would restore neither damages nor a particular allocation and reject both automatic newsletter immunity and automatic loss of protection for an offensive editorial.

### 1997-01-06 — United States v. Watts; United States v. Putra; No. 95-1906, one Rule 12.4 petition concerning two Ninth Circuit judgments

**Justice Scalia, concurring; no joins.** He joins the bounded Court opinion, which does not say that every punishment below a statutory ceiling is necessarily punishment only for the conviction. His additional disagreement concerns Commission authority. In his view, §994(b)(1)'s requirement of consistency with pertinent provisions of Title 18 and §3661's protection of sentencing-information consideration forbid a Commission or judicial rule excluding otherwise lawful acquitted-conduct consideration. The Commission may recommend congressional change; it may not itself prohibit a lawful enhancement or impose an otherwise unsupported higher burden solely because the conduct was acquitted. That statutory objection is his own; Thomas's agreement with the narrow constitutional opinion supplies no join to it.

**Justice Breyer, concurring; no joins.** He joins the Court's construction of the Guidelines as written and its constitutional holding. He regards the use of acquitted conduct in mandatory enhancement as a legitimate subject of Commission policy change. Different burdens make judicial findings compatible with acquittals, but that is not the only permissible sentencing-policy consideration. The institutional significance of a jury's acquittal may support excluding that conduct from mandatory enhancement even though the present relevant-conduct provisions contain no such exception. He disagrees with Scalia's proposed statutory restriction on the Commission. Neither concurrence changes today's calculation rules.

**Justice Stevens, dissenting; no joins.** He seeks plenary briefing and argument and would, if the merits are decided now, affirm both sentence-vacatur judgments. Section 3661 permits receiving information and using it in lawful sentencing discretion; it does not itself assign mandatory weight or authorize a binding-range increase on a preponderance finding of additional criminal conduct. Section 1B1.4 addresses selection within the range or departure, while §1B1.3 determines the range through relevant conduct. Section 994(l)'s instruction about incremental punishment for multiple convictions reinforces his narrower authorization reading; the Court's contrary view treats that instruction as a minimum rather than an exclusive limit.

The criminal proof tradition and his McMillan dissent make the mandatory punitive consequence central. His Witte dissent likewise rejects the notion that a broad statutory maximum erases the concrete increment. He distinguishes discretionary use of information from facts that enlarge a binding range, and would not sustain these increases on the existing preponderance findings. In Watts, possession and use differ; his objection does not depend on a finding that the jury rejected possession. He announces no categorical ban on considering an acquitted episode, no independent Grady successive-prosecution bar, and no comprehensive new jury-allocation test. Lawful resentencing may use information in selecting an authorized sentence, but may not simply reimpose these mandatory increases on the same insufficient authorization-and-proof premise. He sets no sentence and would disturb no acquittal.

**Justice Kennedy, dissenting; no joins.** He would receive full merits briefing and oral argument before resolving this important recurring question. Dowling and Witte make the Government's objection to a categorical bar persuasive, and circuit conflict supports review. But Witte expressly reserved acquitted conduct; mandatory sentencing gives the distinction practical force, and disagreement among the reversal supporters about the Commission's authority exposes an unsettled statutory issue. Summary correction with reservations does not provide the examination he considers necessary. He neither affirms the defendants' merits position nor adopts a reasonable-doubt rule; his present dissent concerns the procedure of deciding the merits now.

### 1997-01-07 — Old Chief v. United States; No. 95-6556

**Chief Justice Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and dissenting in part; no joins.** He joins the Rule 403 holding and reversal because the comparison is between two means of proving the same complete legal status, not between proof and no proof. Ordinary prosecutorial narrative control has limited force for status detached from the charged episode. An unconditional, legally complete admission supplies that element, while identifying the similar assault adds no narrative link to present possession and creates acute propensity danger. He preserves the Government's ability to prove a distinct nonpropensity purpose under Rule 403 and rejects any general right to stipulate away event narrative or require acceptance of partial or qualified admissions.

He differs on remedy. In his view, the close resemblance to violent conduct and the unnecessary character information prevent the Government from showing harmlessness on this record. He would vacate the conviction and remand for a new trial rather than leave harmlessness open. At retrial the Government could use the adequate admission or another sanitized means for status; prior-offense details could be introduced only for a distinct lawful purpose satisfying Rule 403. His prejudice conclusion and mandatory new-trial remedy command no additional join and do not change the Court's five-Justice remand.

**Justice O'Connor, dissenting, joined by Justices Scalia and Thomas.** They would affirm because the authentic judgment directly proves a statutory element. A defendant's offer neither removes that element nor makes ordinary specific proof irrelevant; the Government retains its burden and its legitimate interest in persuasive evidence. Huddleston's safeguards and the Rule's substantial-outweighing requirement preserve meaningful trial discretion. They recognize the similar-assault propensity danger but would not find the name and basic nature of this qualifying conviction inadmissible as a matter of law merely because an admission proves the same legal status. They question the compulsory-substitution consequence and the sharp distinction between status proof and narrative proof, without treating relevance as conclusive admissibility or prosecutorial choice as immune from Rule 403.

They do not rely on the curable instruction wording as a new ground, and they do not treat the credibility instruction as waiver of the separate objection. Once the Court's error rule governs, they accept the ordinary Williamson/Kotteakos harmlessness process and oppose automatic retrial; that conditional remedy position is not a vote to find error or reverse. No omitted-element constitutional error or Roy substitute standard is claimed.

### 1997-01-13 — Walmer v. Department of Defense; Tenth Circuit No. 93-3377, 52 F.3d 851; no separate Supreme Court docket supplied

**Justice Scalia, concurring, joined by Justice Thomas.** They join both Court parts and regard the specific military relationship as sufficient. They also draw on Bowers's recognition of authority to regulate the specified conduct: a reasonable conduct-based personnel policy may rest on a permissible moral judgment as well as military discipline. Their Romer dissent distinguished such judgment from a bare wish to harm persons. They do not claim that Bowers already decided equal protection, that every private aversion is legitimate or that the Court has overruled Romer. Beach's tolerance for reasonable predictions and imperfect fit supports this narrower service policy. No individual-performance finding or least restrictive alternative is required. This additional conduct-morality ground is theirs alone and is not attributed to the other three equality affirmers.

**Justice Souter, concurring in part and dissenting in part, joined by Justices Stevens and Ginsburg.** They join the attainder holding but would vacate the equality-based denial and remand. Heller and Romer require examination of the connection between this actual disadvantage and a legitimate objective. Rich concerned fraudulent denial on entry under another regulation, so treating it as conclusive leaves this admitted-acts classification insufficiently examined. Stevens's Beach position likewise requires a relationship to the actual distinction, and Ginsburg's Virginia position supports applying the proper inquiry without importing that case's sex-classification tier.

They accept substantial deference to reasonable military predictions, the availability of conceivable legitimate reasons and Walmer's burden to establish entitlement to preliminary relief. They find legal inadequacy in foreclosure by the older case, not proof that the Army lacks a rational basis. They demand neither actual-purpose proof from the Government, heightened scrutiny, an individualized impairment finding nor a new evidentiary hearing. On remand the courts should reassess the merits question under ordinary rationality and address irreparable injury, comparative harm and public interest if the renewed merits assessment makes them material. Those factors were never found satisfied. They would neither enjoin separation automatically nor finally invalidate the policy.

**Chief Justice Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and dissenting in part; no joins.** He joins the legislative-predicate attainder holding and would vacate the equality-based denial under a different inquiry. His Part A treats mandatory separation for homosexual acts as an intentional sexual-orientation classification, whether described as conduct or a deliberate status proxy. Bowers does not exempt it from equality review. Romer supplies an ordinary-review floor and a warning against unexplained class disadvantage, but does not itself allocate a justification burden to the Government. He would make that doctrinal change here: the Government must identify an actual military objective and establish a real relationship between it and the intentional classification, without relying on moral disapproval, private bias or stereotype.

His reason is that merely conceivable explanations would permit this intentional disadvantage without establishing its actual connection to the military function invoked. Professional judgments and reasonable contemporaneous predictions about discipline, cohesion, readiness and command receive substantial but nonconclusive weight; an assertion of deference does not carry the Government's burden. Experience and institutional knowledge may suffice without scientific certainty or a universal formal-findings requirement. Part A independently supports his remand because the lower courts treated the claim as foreclosed, placed the practical burden on Walmer to disprove the rule, and did not resolve the military justification his proposed allocation requires.

His separable Part B additionally adopts intermediate scrutiny: the Government must identify an actual important military objective and establish a substantial relationship to it, with substantial weight to supported professional judgment. Neither Romer nor the public-university sex cases already supplies that tier. Separating Part B leaves Part A's independent Government burden intact.

He retains Bowers's specified-conduct holding, ordinary regulation of materially relevant conduct and the absence of a constitutional entitlement to service. He requires neither least restrictive means nor an individual exception in every case, and he does not infer that military concerns lack support from the absence of an individual performance finding. The district court should assess the military showing on a developed record and apply all preliminary-relief requirements. He would order no injunction, immediate status change or final invalidation. Any concrete personnel commitments or settled arrangements must be shown in the actual record and given their proper remedial weight; abstract command responsibility, convenience, institutional preference or expected continued exclusion does not establish protected reliance. He makes no finding here that such commitments exist and adds no automatic transition requirement. His Part A burden and Part B tier each remain noncontrolling.

### 1997-01-14 — Abebe-Jira v. Negewo, No. 95-8873; Eleventh Circuit No. 93-9133.

Justice Scalia, joined by Justice Thomas, concurs in Parts I and V and dissents from the damages judgment. They accept the statutory forum and reject a categorical political-question bar, but find no sufficient congressional authority for the asserted domestic damages action. The prohibition of torture does not itself authorize a federal cause of action. A forum for independently actionable law-of-nations torts does not necessarily authorize judicial recognition of every later norm; the common-law setting and lower-court practice are the strongest affirmative arguments, but do not establish the needed source for these Justices.

Suter requires an actual source of private liability; O'Melveny rejects the manufacture of a federal rule from general federal interests; Meyer keeps jurisdiction and substantive action distinct. Franklin presupposed a cognizable action, and their concurrence there relied on a narrower enacted-remedies ground. Central Bank's binding received-securities holding remains confined to its established setting, and Musick, Peeler concerns incidents of already recognized liability. Neither supplies the missing ATS premise. Sanchez-Espinoza's domestic-immunity result is not a categorical bar to foreign-official suits. Scalia and Thomas would reverse the damages judgment and remand on the absence-of-action ground, rejecting both compensation and punishment through that ground. They announce no categorical objection to punitive damages in an otherwise authorized intentional-tort action, do not approve torture, and do not reach an unpleaded TVPA claim, limitations or appointed-counsel question.

### 1997-01-21 - Babbitt v. Youpee, No. 95-1595; OT1996.

Authority: [Record](../records/Babbitt_v_Youpee_merits_1997-01-21.md).

Justice Stevens dissents. His concurrence in Irving accepted Congress's power to impose consolidation conditions but objected to their abrupt application without a reasonable opportunity to arrange affairs. Texaco v. Short supports allowing an owner time to avoid a legislated loss. Youpee died nearly six years after the October 30, 1984 amendment, which preserved lifetime use and transfer, permitted devise to an existing co-owner, and narrowed the affected interests through its earnings provisions. Stevens regards those changes and that opportunity as sufficient to distinguish Irving.

The difficulty of transmitting these interests to family members is substantial, but Stevens would not turn ordinary beneficiary choice into a right to continue existing fractionation indefinitely. The fact that these particular devises do not create additional fractions does not foreclose legislation directed at reducing the existing problem. He would reverse and remand on the presented takings ground, without ordering a new probate distribution or deciding an individualized notice claim. He does not find that Youpee actually knew of the statute, culpably abandoned the interests, or held property of no value. He also rejects extending Lucas to every restriction of a separate property attribute.
